Federal circuit courts of appeals are increasingly confronting a significant and evolving question in immigration law: whether a noncitizen who entered the United States without inspection and is later arrested in the interior may be subject to mandatory detention under INA § 235(b)(2)(A), or whether INA § 236(a) applies and makes the noncitizen eligible for an individualized bond hearing before an immigration judge.

# Habeas Corpus-Bond Eligibility-Immigration Detention
**7^th Circuit Court of Appeals**

**Case Name: Jaciel Rojas v. Samuel Olson**

**Case No.: 25-3127**

**Officials: Sykes, Jackson-Akiwumi, and Kolar, Circuit Judges.**
**Focus: Habeas Corpus-Bond Eligibility-Immigration Detention**

After entering the United States without inspection in 2018, Rojas, a Mexican national, was arrested by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in 2025. DHS initially detained him under 8 U.S.C. § 1226, and an immigration judge determined that he posed neither a danger to the community nor a flight risk, ordering his release on bond pending removal proceedings.
DHS later changed its position in light of new agency guidance, arguing that Rojas was instead subject to mandatory detention under 8 U.S.C. § 1225(b)(2)(A), which requires detention without bond for certain applicants for admission. During the removal proceedings, Rojas applied for asylum, withholding of removal, and protection under the Convention Against Torture.
The Seventh Circuit reviewed the district court’s decision de novo, and at first concluded that the case was not moot because DHS had represented that it would re-detain Rojas if the BIA’s decision remained in effect. On the merits, the court held that § 1225(b)(2)(A) applies only to noncitizens who are both “applicants for admission” and “seeking admission,” construing the latter phrase according to its ordinary meaning.
Because Rojas was not seeking admission but instead sought forms of humanitarian relief that do not constitute an application for admission, he was not subject to mandatory detention under § 1225(b)(2)(A). The court held that his detention was governed by § 1226, under which he was entitled to an individualized bond hearing. Accordingly, the Seventh Circuit reversed the district court’s denial of habeas relief and remanded with instructions to grant the writ.

# Seventh Circuit Rejects DHS Reading That Would Deny Immigration Detention Bond Hearings
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit ruled Thursday that noncitizens arrested in the interior of the United States are detained under 8 U.S.C. § 1226 and remain eligible for an immigration detention bond hearing, rejecting the Department of Homeland Security’s position that § 1225(b)(2)(A) requires their mandatory detention without a hearing.
The Seventh Circuit’s opinion in Cirrus Rojas v. Olson, No. 25-3127 arose from the habeas petition of Jaciel Cirrus Rojas, who has lived in the United States since 2018. DHS initially arrested him under § 1226, and an immigration judge, applying the same provision, found him neither a danger nor a flight risk and ordered him released on bond.
## Why Interior Arrests Keep Their Bond Hearings
The Seventh Circuit rejected the government’s reading and held that § 1226 governs the detention of noncitizens arrested in the interior, preserving their access to bond hearings before an immigration judge. The panel framed the question as narrow but consequential, writing that it “determines whether millions of aliens living in the United States are subject to mandatory detention, or are eligible for bond hearings before an immigration judge.”
The opinion catalogs the circuits that have addressed the question and notes that a consensus is emerging against the government’s position. The Seventh Circuit joined the Second, Sixth, Tenth, and Eleventh Circuits in rejecting DHS’s interpretation. The Fifth and Eighth Circuits have adopted it, each over a dissent.

linkup.snippet:
Last month, the Seventh Circuit in *Cirrus Rojas v. Olson* held the opposite: Deeming a longtime resident an applicant for admission doesn’t make him one seeking it, so [Section 1226(a)](https://www.bloomberglaw.com/public/document/USCode8USC1226Apprehensionanddetentionofaliens/1?doc_id=XEH10E003) governs and a bond hearing is available.
The Seventh Circuit answered in *Cirrus Rojas v. Olson* that a legal fiction travels only as far as its text. Congress defined “applicant for admission” but left “seeking admission” undefined, so ordinary meaning controls. Jaciel Cirrus Rojas — in the country since 2018 and pursuing asylum and related protection, not lawful entry — isn’t seeking admission in any ordinary sense, and deeming him an applicant doesn’t “conjure a fictional intent to seek admission,” Judge Joshua Kolar wrote.  
Structure agreed: The [2025 Laken Riley Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/5)’s expansion of Section 1226(c)’s detention list would be pointless if Section 1225 already required detaining every unlawful entrant, and Congress never funded the mass detention now read into a 1996 catchall. Judge Diane Sykes dissented, siding with the Fifth and Eighth Circuits, saying that the statute classifies people like Cirrus Rojas as constructively seeking admission.
The Seventh Circuit saw the same problem. Two immigration judges found Cirrus Rojas neither a flight risk nor a danger, yet the government insists on confinement, the purposeless deprivation *Zadvydas v. Davis* warns against.

The government’s argument that noncitizens living in the US are nevertheless “seeking admission” to the country, just like those crossing at the border, doesn’t hold water, wrote Judge Joshua Kolar in Thursday’s opinion . That claim “rests upon the illogical use of both legal fiction and ordinary meaning for the same term,” he said.

Such hearings aren’t available to those apprehended while “seeking admission.”
Last year, however, the administration began to interpret the law such that even unauthorized immigrants who have lived in the US for years are “seeking admission” and subject to mandatory detention.
Jaciel Cirrus Rojas, the petitioner in the underlying district court case, “has never applied for anything that counts as ‘admission’ to the United States. A federal appeals court in Chicago on Thursday rejected the Trump administration’s mandatory detention policy for immigrants in removal proceedings, ending its split over a year-old policy that has prevented thousands of immigrants in federal custody from requesting bond.

The 2-1 decision may allow hundreds of detainees in Illinois, Indiana and Wisconsin — the three states within the court’s jurisdiction — to seek bond hearings in immigration court.

The Seventh Circuit’s opinion in Cirrus Rojas v. Olson, No. 25-3127 arose from the habeas petition of Jaciel Cirrus Rojas, who has lived in the United States since 2018. DHS initially arrested him under § 1226, and an immigration judge, applying the same provision, found him neither a danger nor a flight risk and ordered him released on bond.
The Seventh Circuit ruled July 30 that noncitizens arrested in the U.S. interior stay eligible for bond hearings under § 1226, rejecting DHS's § 1225 theory.
Wisconsin Watch, in coverage of the Seventh Circuit ruling, reported that the decision could allow hundreds of detainees in Wisconsin, Indiana, and Illinois to seek bond hearings after prolonged mandatory detention. Courthouse News, in its report on the Ninth Circuit decision, described the Trump administration’s July 2025 guidance as extending to interior detainees the no-bail rule long applied to those apprehended at the border. Cirrus Rojas remained detained at Dodge County Jail in Wisconsin during the appeal.
The Seventh Circuit rejected the government’s reading and held that § 1226 governs the detention of noncitizens arrested in the interior, preserving their access to bond hearings before an immigration judge.

you.snippet:
Judge Lee’s opinion rejected the government’s position that noncitizens apprehended within the interior after entering without inspection are categorically subject to mandatory detention, reasoning that such individuals are not actively “seeking admission.” However, the panel did not produce a majority holding on the statutory question because Judge Pryor concurred separately and concluded the court need not resolve the issue. Accordingly, Castañon-Nava itself did not definitively resolve the statutory question. The Seventh Circuit subsequently did so in Cirrus Rojas v. Olson. Jaciel Cirrus Rojas v. Samuel Olson, 25-3127, (7th Cir.)
Federal circuit courts of appeals are increasingly confronting a significant and evolving question in immigration law: whether a noncitizen who entered the United States without inspection and is later arrested in the interior may be subject to mandatory detention under INA § 235(b)(2)(A), or whether INA § 236(a) applies and makes the noncitizen eligible for an individualized bond hearing before an immigration judge.
The Seventh Circuit held that he was not "seeking admission" within the meaning of the INA because admission means "lawful entry...into the United States after inspection and authorization." As a result, the court reasoned that noncitizens in Cirrus Rojas' position "can only seek to remain in the United States through other forms of relief that are not admission."
By contrast, the First, Second, Third, Fourth, Sixth, Seventh, Ninth, Tenth, and Eleventh Circuits have concluded that noncitizens who entered without inspection and are later apprehended in the interior are generally not “seeking admission” for purposes of INA § 235(b)(2)(A) and instead fall within INA § 236(a), subject to other applicable mandatory-detention provisions, making them generally eligible for individualized bond hearings.
